Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

cope verb

also cope with, I can’t cope, be up to it, be equal to, deal with (a burden), handle (a situation), unable to cope, be up to a task

classical

Plin. Ep. 3.17.2: cui pār esse nōn possum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Att. 12.15: sed adhūc parēs nōn sumus (Lewis & Short: “not equal to the task”)
Traupman 150, 297

pār esse

phrase: pār, paris, adjective, with esse and the dative

be equal to, be a match for; cope with

Latin says that one is, or is not, a match for the thing: a task, a worry, a grief, an enemy. Pār is first of all “equal” and, as a noun, “a pair”; pār est means “it is right, fitting” (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • impār esse — be unequal to, be unable to cope with

    phrase: impār, imparis, adjective, with esse and the dative · also used · classical · Hor. C. 4.6.5: tibi mīles impār (Lewis & Short); Traupman 150, 297; Traupman 297

    Lewis & Short: in this sense perhaps not before the Augustan age; Cicero and Pliny say pār nōn esse. Its first sense is “unequal, uneven” (an odd number).

Examples

  • exime hunc mihi scrūpulum, cui pār esse nōn possum

    take this worry off me: I can’t cope with itPlin. Ep. 3.17.2 (Lewis & Short)

  • cui repugnō, quoad possum, sed adhūc parēs nōn sumus

    I fight it (my grief) as far as I can, but so far I am not equal to itCic. Att. 12.15 (Lewis & Short)

  • Sōlus huic negōtiō pār nōn sum; adjuvā mē.

    I can’t cope with this on my own; help me.composed

  • operī pār esse

    to be up to a taskTraupman 277

See also suffer, manage, difficult.

SourcesLewis & Short: par · Lewis & Short: impar

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 150, 297.
